title: Humbled in Belfast, India Arrive in England With Questions They Cannot Ignore
excerpt: After a historic 0-2 whitewash by Ireland, Shreyas Iyer's India face a full-strength England in a five-match T20I series starting Wednesday. The biggest question: will Vaibhav Sooryavanshi finally play?
body:
The double T20 world champions are heading to England. They are doing so without a shred of momentum.

India's 0-2 whitewash at the hands of Ireland in Belfast — a team they had never lost to in international cricket — has sent shockwaves through Indian cricket. Assistant coach Ryan ten Doeschate, himself a former Dutch international who knows British and Irish conditions intimately, could barely process what had happened.

"There's a little bit of disbelief," he told reporters after Sunday's one-run defeat sealed the series. "It's also very hard to be critical of guys who have just won a World Cup. We've been outdone or outsmarted by a team who just did the basics very well."

The basics. That is what undid India. On spicier pitches with bigger square boundaries — a world away from the flat decks and short ropes of the Indian Premier League — Iyer's batters could not adjust. And ten Doeschate knows England will offer no respite.

"We're probably too used to a tempo and style where you can hit sixes more freely," he said. "I think this will be the case when you go to England as well — maybe slightly quicker wickets, maybe slightly less wind, but we're going to have to adapt and be a lot smarter about how we'd like to play if we're going to get wins there."

## Five matches, five English grounds, one massive question

The tour opens on Wednesday, July 1, at the Banks Homes Riverside in Chester-le-Street, Durham. Four more T20Is follow — at Old Trafford in Manchester on July 4, Trent Bridge in Nottingham on July 7, Bristol's Seat Unique Stadium on July 9, and the Utilita Bowl in Southampton on July 11. For the Indian diaspora in the UK, these matches represent a rare chance to see their national team play live, bringing a palpable buzz to cities with large South Asian populations.

England will be at full strength and on home turf. Jos Buttler captains a side featuring Harry Brook, Will Jacks, Phil Salt, and a returning Jofra Archer, whose raw pace against Indian batters on English soil could be the series-defining factor. Sam Curran, Adil Rashid, and Jacob Bethell add depth and variety. This is not Ireland.

## The Sooryavanshi question

The elephant in the room is Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. The 15-year-old left-hander won the Orange Cap in IPL 2026 with a staggering 776 runs at a strike rate of 237.30, hammering 72 sixes across the tournament. He is the most talked-about cricketer in the country. And yet India benched him for both T20Is against Ireland.

Both matches. Both losses.

The decision not to play Sooryavanshi has drawn fierce criticism. Sunil Gavaskar, speaking on Sports Tak, was unequivocal: "I think he has to be included in the very first match. It's as simple as that. Keep the batters who are out of form out of the playing XI and play Vaibhav Suryavanshi instead."

Gavaskar added: "Either open with him or bat him at No. 3. But one thing is certain — he has to play the first match against England on July 1. If India wants to surprise England in the very first match, Vaibhav Suryavanshi has to play. If he gets going in the opening match, England will be shaken."

England are already planning for him. Former captain Michael Vaughan has suggested a specific tactical counter: win the toss, choose to bat first, and make Sooryavanshi field for an entire innings before he gets to the crease.

"The one thing he's going to have to cope with is his fielding," Vaughan said on Ajinkya Rahane's YouTube channel. "There's no impact sub where he can sit on the bench. If I was England, I'd ask India to field first because then by the time Suryavanshi comes to bat, he might be tired."

That England's pre-series strategy revolves around neutralising a 15-year-old tells you everything about how much Sooryavanshi has shifted the calculus of Indian cricket. His inclusion, or lack thereof, will be a major talking point among fans globally, including those following from the US and Canada.

## Iyer's captaincy under the microscope

Shreyas Iyer's debut as India's T20I captain could not have gone worse. A clean sweep by Ireland — the first team outside the traditional powers to whitewash India in a bilateral T20 series — raises serious questions about his tactical acumen and his ability to inspire under pressure.

In the second T20I, Ireland's Jai Moondra dismissed India's top three — Sanju Samson, Abhishek Sharma, and Iyer himself — inside the first three overs, leaving India reeling at 19 for 3. Only Tilak Varma's fighting 55 kept India in the hunt, but it was not enough.

Iyer acknowledged the damage: "Kudos to them, the way they played. Showed professionalism, they had tremendous idea of how the wicket was going to play."

The captain will need to show more than graciousness in defeat. He needs runs, tactical clarity, and — most critically — the courage to play his best XI. India's squad for the England T20Is includes Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson, Tilak Varma, Abhishek Sharma, Ravi Bishnoi, Varun Chakravarthy, Arshdeep Singh, Harshit Rana, and the uncapped Suryansh Shedge. There is no shortage of talent. But Belfast showed that talent without adaptability is worthless.

## Ireland's triumph in context

Ireland's win was not a fluke. It was the culmination of years of patient development under Heinrich Malan, who announced his departure as head coach on Monday — stepping down on the highest note imaginable. Malan oversaw Ireland's qualification for three consecutive T20 World Cups, their first Test victories, and now their first series win against India.

His successor, Gary Wilson, becomes the first Irish-born head coach in over 30 years. The transition is a reminder that cricket's smaller nations are no longer pushovers. For India, the lesson is uncomfortable but unmistakable: World Cup titles do not guarantee results in conditions that demand adjustment. This humbling experience serves as a stark reminder for the team and its global fanbase, including NRIs who often follow these tours with immense national pride.

## What NRIs in Britain should know

For the Indian diaspora in the United Kingdom — an estimated 1.8 million people of Indian origin — this tour is one of the few annual opportunities to watch India play live without crossing continents. Durham, Manchester, Nottingham, Bristol, and Southampton are all accessible cities with significant South Asian communities. The matches will be broadcast on Sky Sports and available for streaming.

The first T20I in Durham begins at 5:30 PM local time (10 PM IST, 12:30 PM ET) on Wednesday. After the shame of Belfast, India arrive knowing that the NRI cricket faithful will be watching — and expecting far more than what they got from Ireland.

**India T20I squad for England:** Shreyas Iyer (c), Sanju Samson (wk), Ishan Kishan (wk), Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Shivam Dube, Suryansh Shedge, Axar Patel, Washington Sundar, Ravi Bishnoi, Varun Chakravarthy, Arshdeep Singh, Harshit Rana, Prasidh Krishna, Prince Yadav

**England T20I squad:** Jos Buttler (c, wk), Phil Salt (wk), Jordan Cox (wk), Harry Brook, Will Jacks, Tom Banton, Jacob Bethell, Sam Curran, James Coles, Liam Dawson, Rehan Ahmed, Jofra Archer, Saqib Mahmood, Josh Tongue, Luke Wood, Sonny Baker, Adil Rashid

**Schedule:**
- 1st T20I: July 1, Durham (Banks Homes Riverside)
- 2nd T20I: July 4, Manchester (Old Trafford)
- 3rd T20I: July 7, Nottingham (Trent Bridge)
- 4th T20I: July 9, Bristol (Seat Unique Stadium)
- 5th T20I: July 11, Southampton (Utilita Bowl)
